title: NASA's OSIRIS-APEX Spacecraft Could Intercept the Mysterious Object 1998 KY26 in June 2037

--

In recent interviews (here, here, here, here and a tweet with a million views here), I explained that the so-called “dark comet” 1998 KY26 might be the lost soviet spacecraft, Phobos 1. This argument is based on the detailed quantitative analysis presented in two papers that I co-authored with Adam Hibberd and Adam Crawl, which were posted here and here.

Needless to say, I was disappointed when the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) announced here on November 14, 2026 that they “decided to abandon its plan to reach asteroid 1998 KY26, the final destination of the Hayabusa2 probe. The decision was made due to engine problems that significantly exceeded the design life, and the probe will now head to a different asteroid.”

But the prospects of an intercept are not lost. In a new paper that I co-authored with Adam Hibberd, available here, we show that NASA’s mission OSIRIS-APEX (formerly OSIRIS-REx) could intercept 1998 KY26 after completing its science mission at Apophis. We calculate that a velocity thrust ∆V of 180 meters per second on 17 February 2034, followed by a minor deep-space maneuver of a meter per second and a passive Earth gravity assist, enables a flyby of 1998 KY26 on 25 June 2037 at a relative velocity of 5.6 kilometers per second. The total required ∆V of 181 meters per second is below the published estimated reserve in fuel of approximately 206 meters per second following proximity operations at Apophis.

A video animation of our calculated orbit of the OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft up to its encounter with 1998 KY26 is available here.

The mysterious object 1998 KY26, categorized as a ’dark comet’ because of its many unusual properties, is extremely appealing as a target for a spacecraft mission. A flyby is probably the only way its various mysterious characteristics can be explained. Amongst these are its non-gravitational accelerations, namely the presence of perturbing forces that cannot be explained by gravity alone.

We addressed an alternative option to flyby 1998 KY26 by exploiting an existing and currently active interplanetary NASA spacecraft, OSIRIS-APEX, now on its way to rendezvous the potentially hazardous asteroid (99942) Apophis before and just after Apophis’s close perigee on 13th April 2029. The proposed mission would divert the OSIRIS-APEX probe to 1998 KY26 after completion of its scientific mission at Apophis.

The epoch at which intercept of the target occurs in 2037 is more than a decade from now, and it is up to the NASA team responsible to decide whether this is feasible in the context of budget, logistics, spacecraft lifetime, and ∆V requirement.

The arrival geometry of OSIRIS-APEX at 1998 KY26 requires attention. The solar elongation of the spacecraft as viewed from Earth would be ∼ 14◦, which is reasonable. Also, although the solar phase of the target is almost 180◦ (indicating the target is almost completely silhouetted), this reverses to only ∼ 0◦ after closest approach, meaning that the object is almost entirely lit, leading to excellent viewing conditions. Furthermore, the transition between these two extremes at closest approach could potentially permit the detection of surface features at a useful resolution. However, the solar elongation of 1998 KY26 with respect to the probe at intercept is only ∼ 6◦, which would be problematic as far as navigation from optical sightings and other important spacecraft activities are concerned.

Our proposal to NASA can be taken up by extending the OSIRIS-APEX operations until late June 2037, when a flyby of this object can be conducted. The mission involves an application of a velocity boost of ∆V of 180 meters per second on 17th February 2034, comfortably within the scope remaining in the probe’s fuel tanks after the scientific exploration of Apophis is over.

***

The proposed encounter of OSIRIS-APEX with 1998 KY26 is important for the following reasons.

Dark comets are a hypothesized class of curious hybrids between comets and asteroids. These objects show significant non-gravitational accelerations, yet they exhibit absolutely no sign of cometary outgassing in the form of a coma or tail. The first recognized interstellar object, `Oumuamua, showed these features and was suggested to be a `dark comet’ in recent mainstream publications, such as here. However, based on its inferred flat shape (published here) and non-gravitational acceleration (published here), I argued 8 years ago here that `Oumuamua might be pushed by sunlight and is technological in origin. The dark comet categorization of `Oumuamua and similar solar system objects was the mainstream response to my non-traditional suggestion.

What is the evidence for the possible association of the so-called “dark comet” 1998 KY26 with the spacecraft Phobos 1?”

First, the orbit of 1998 KY26 is very close to that of the Russian probe Phobos 1, which suffered a failure 2 months after the launch in July 1988, due to upload of a faulty command. The first paper I co-authored here shows that by matching the trajectories of Phobos 1 and 1998 KY26. Indeed, a recent paper here reported that the interior of 1998 KY26 is too hot for a comet.

Second, 1998 KY26 exhibits a non-gravitational push away from the Sun with no detectable shedding of gas or dust, as expected from the rocket effect of a comet. Our second paper here explains this push as the result of the reflection of sunlight by the solar panels of Phobos 1. Remarkably, we found that the anomalous non-gravitational acceleration and the brightness variation of 1998 KY26 can both be explained by the reflection of sunlight from Phobos 1 with its solar panels.

Recent radar and optical observations of 1998 KY26 indicate an unusually rapid spin-rate with a period of 5.35 minutes which is much faster than a natural pile of rocks glued by can sustain. The observations also implied a diameter of order 10 meters, and a shiny surface which reflects 52% of the sunlight impinging on it, both facts that are consistent with expectations from the Phobos 1 spacecraft.

The stakes for `Oumuamua being technological in origin are much higher than for 1998 KY26, because its high speed cannot be of human origin. Realizing that 1998 KY26 is technological rather than a `dark comet’ would suggest the possibility `Oumuamua is the first encounter of astronomers with alien technology.
